name: Trademark Filing and Specimens
title: Trademark Filing and Specimens
answer: Trademark filing and specimens covers the steps a business takes to seek registration of a mark and to prove that the mark is actually used in commerce. It includes choosing the filing basis, describing the goods or services, submitting a drawing of the mark, and providing a specimen such as a label, tag, packaging, website screenshot, or point of sale display. The scope also reaches office actions, responses, publication, opposition, registration, and the later maintenance filings that keep a registration alive. In an AI context, the same scope applies when the mark covers software, models, data services, or AI generated outputs, and when the specimen itself is a digital interface or an online advertisement.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Trademark filing runs on the electronic systems of trademark offices, such as the USPTO, WIPO's Madrid System, and equivalent national or regional portals. It also runs on docketing and IP management software, document management, and increasingly on AI assisted search and classification tools that help pick Nice classes and compare goods and services descriptions. Specimens live as image files, PDFs, URLs, and screen captures, so the infrastructure includes web archiving, version control, and secure storage for evidence. For AI related marks, the infrastructure may also include model cards, product screenshots, and logs that show the mark in use with the claimed services.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A practitioner clears the mark, selects the filing basis, drafts the goods and services identification, and prepares a specimen that shows the mark as used by the applicant in commerce. For use based filings, the specimen must match the mark and the goods or services, and it must show a real sale or offering, not a mockup or a mere internal document. For intent to use filings, the specimen comes later with an amendment to allege use or a statement of use. AI tools can help review specimen images, flag mismatches, and draft office action responses, but a human still checks the legal sufficiency and the factual accuracy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The applicant must own the mark, control the quality of goods or services under it, and keep records that show the specimen's origin, date, and context. Risks include specimen fraud, false claims of use, overbroad goods and services, and conflicts with earlier marks or rights of publicity. Provenance matters because a specimen pulled from a marketplace, a competitor's page, or an AI generated mockup can invalidate a filing or expose the applicant to fraud claims. The site's tracker counts 147 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which is a reminder that trademark filings around AI products can sit close to active disputes. Governance also includes monitoring, watch notices, and internal approval for how AI generated content is labeled and used as evidence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Trademark offices are moving toward more structured data, image recognition for logo search, and machine readable goods and services lists. AI generated specimens and AI assisted drafting will likely increase scrutiny, so examiners and courts may demand clearer proof that a mark was used in real commerce. Expect more guidance on how to submit digital specimens, such as app screens, chat interfaces, and model outputs, and on how to document provenance for those files. The field will also track the growing body of AI case law as those decisions shape what counts as use and what counts as evidence.
